- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. requirements) is recorded here. If it is not in the contract, it does not exist.

---

## What is in this folder

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `[prefix]-contract.js` | The contract: an array of component definitions. Generated and maintained by `/extract`. |
| `validate.mjs` | Checks the atomic model rules against the contract. Run before any handover. |

---

## How to read a contract entry

```js
{
  name:      "Button",          // PascalCase component name
  prefix:    "ds",              // tag namespace (from project.config.js)
  element:   "ds-button",       // the custom element tag
  atomic:    "atom",            // atom | molecule | organism
  composes:  [],                // elements this component renders in its own template
  attributes: [
    { name: "variant", type: "enum",    values: ["primary","secondary","ghost"], default: "primary" },
    { name: "size",    type: "enum",    values: ["sm","md","lg"],                default: "md" },
    { name: "disabled",type: "boolean",                                          default: false },
  ],
  slots: [
    { name: "default", description: "Button label text" },
  ],
  a11y:      "role=button, aria-disabled when disabled, keyboard: Enter and Space activate",
  status:    "final",           // draft | in-review | final
  extracted: "2026-07-07",
}
```

**`atomic`**: the component's tier, determined by what it renders in its own template:
- `atom`: renders no other component. `composes: []`.
- `molecule`: renders only atoms.
- `organism`: renders at least one molecule.

`template` and `page` are not valid contract tiers. They are layout-layer deliverables, not Custom Elements. See atomic model Rule F in `.claude/skills/_shared/atomic-model.md`.

**`composes`**: what the component's own template renders. Slotted children are not listed here (see atomic model Rule B). This determines the tier and build order: build atoms first, then molecules, then organisms.

- `enum`: a fixed set of values. Use the `default` if none is passed or the value is unrecognised.

- `string`: freeform content.

**`slots`**: named `"default"` is the element's child content. Named slots use `slot="[name]"` on a child element.

---

2. Build one Custom Element per entry. The `element` value is the tag to register.
3. `composes` → your imports. Build those components first.
4. `attributes` → your `observedAttributes` array and prop defaults.
5. `slots` → your shadow DOM slot elements.
6. `a11y` → bake in. Assert in tests.

   No hardcoded values.

Here's the full picture, top-down. This is long because you asked for mastery — treat each section as a layer you can stop at, or tell me which one to go deeper on.

## 1. What this actually is

This repo is a running instance of **"DDP Design OS"** — a templated, AI-driven workflow for Accenture Song design/delivery teams — populated with one real project: **Zimmermann** (a fashion retailer), specifically their **website redesign handover**. Lead is Alrick Pagnon, WCAG AA, targeting **web + React**, component prefix `zimm`.

It is not a codebase in the traditional sense. There's no build, no test suite, no app that runs. It's a **structured knowledge + design-artifact repository** that an AI agent (Claude Code) reads and writes to, following rules baked into `CLAUDE.md`. The output is: token docs, a component library (plain Web Components), specs, HTML/CSS/JS prototypes, and eventually requirements — all converging into a single `05-handover/index.md` that a dev team (you) consumes to build the real product elsewhere.

## 2. The mental model: four independent tracks

| Track | Folder | Triggered by | Status here |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Context** | `01-context/` | Anyone, ad hoc | 2 baseline refs absorbed (zimmermann.com, loewe.com) |
| **Design** | `02-design/` | Designer | Active — 27 components, 17 specs, 3 prototypes |
| **Requirements** | `03-requirements/` | BA/PM | Not started (folder doesn't exist yet, 0 epics/features/stories) |
| **Feedback** | `04-feedback/` | Designer/PM | Not started (folder doesn't exist yet) |

Key point: requirements and design are **explicitly decoupled** — neither blocks the other. This project so far is 100% design-track activity.

## 3. Folder structure, mapped to what's really here

```
01-context/           2 summaries + project-context.md (synthesis) + decisions.md
02-design/
  library/            27 Custom Elements (elements/), tokens.md, common.css, contract/
  specs/              17 component specs, 1 template spec, 0 screens, 0 flows
  prototypes/          3 registered: templates/main, product-listing, product-detail
  catalog/            live browsable index of the library (not yet deployed to Vercel)
  viewer/             prototype viewer shell (not yet deployed to Vercel)
03-requirements/       doesn't exist yet
04-feedback/           doesn't exist yet
05-handover/index.md   the single entry point — "Build Status: Design & Requirements Stage"
```

Everything funnels into `05-handover/index.md` — it's a generated table of contents, not hand-written, and it's what a purely dev-side agent would read first once status flips to "Ready for Build."

## 4. The mechanics of the design system itself

This is the part worth understanding deeply, since you'll be building against it.

**a. Components are plain Web Components, no build step.** Each one is a folder: `elements/button/{zimm-button.js, demo.html, assets/}`. `zimm-button.js` is a vanilla `HTMLElement` subclass with Shadow DOM, `observedAttributes`, and an inline `_render()` — no React, no bundler, no npm install to view it. `prototypeStack` in `project.config.js` is set to `react-cdn` though (React 18 + Babel via CDN, no build) — so prototypes lean React while the library elements themselves are framework-less.

**b. The contract is the actual source of truth**, not the components or specs. `02-design/library/contract/zimm-contract.js` is a 508-line array — one entry per component: name, tag, atomic tier, `composes`, `attributes` (typed, with defaults), `slots`, `a11y` notes. Rule of thumb stated in the contract README: **"if it's not in the contract, it doesn't exist."** I checked, and this is enforced tightly enough that it's already caught a gap: `link` has a library folder *and* a spec (`link.md`) but **no contract entry** — so technically it's not "official" yet. That's a real crack worth flagging to the designer before you build against it.

**c. Atomic model is mechanically defined, not just a convention.** Tier is derived from `composes`: atom = composes nothing, molecule = composes only atoms, organism = composes at least one molecule. `template`/`page` aren't tiers at all — they're layout-only. There's a `validate.mjs` script that checks this automatically (`node 02-design/library/contract/validate.mjs`) — run it before trusting any handover state.

**d. Every spec is two-layer**, split by an HTML comment in the same file: a **design layer** (tokens table, states, variants, a11y, prototype link — designer-owned, e.g. `button.md`) and a **platform layer** at the bottom, currently `[Empty until a developer picks this up.]` — that's literally where you write implementation notes after handover. One file per component, forever — changes are tracked via a changelog block at the top, not new dated files.

**e. Tokens are CSS custom properties** in `common.css` (516 lines) documented in `tokens.md` (360 lines) — colour, typography, spacing, motion, radius. Every component spec cross-references the exact token variables it uses (see `button.md`'s token table). Prototypes can introduce experimental values as "candidates" but `/extract` never silently promotes them into `common.css` without confirmation.

**f. Prototypes carry intent, not just markup.** Each prototype folder has an `intent.md` with frontmatter (`spec:`, `stack:`, `stage:`) plus prose **Why/What/Fidelity** sections. The `product-detail` one, for example, is explicit that it's "wired in Claude, measurements not confirmed from Figma" — meaning it's a plausible-fidelity mock, not a pixel-accurate spec. That distinction matters a lot for you as a dev: prototypes model interaction and flow, they are not guaranteed dimensionally accurate.

## 5. The skill system — the engine that runs all of this

Everything above is produced by 17 slash-command skills living in `.claude/skills/` (`/extract`, `/handover`, `/update-context`, `/workshop`, `/add-to-viewer`, `/requirements-scan`, etc.), each a markdown instruction file read by Claude Code, plus shared logic in `.claude/skills/_shared/` (`atomic-model.md`, `authoring.md`, `portability.md`). `CLAUDE.md` is the constitution — session-start checks, conversational-intake rules (drop a file/URL in chat, it gets absorbed automatically), a missing-path protocol, and a prompt-injection guard for anything ingested from outside the repo. Ownership of each folder is explicitly assigned (designers vs BA/PM vs project lead vs you), so it's worth knowing **you should never hand-edit** the contract, `05-handover/index.md`, `viewer.config.js`, or the design-layer half of any spec.

## 6. Where this project stands right now

- **27 components** built and in the contract: 14 atoms, 10 molecules, 3 organisms — all status `draft` (none `final`).
- **17 of 27** have a written spec; the rest (e.g. `select`, `search`, `card-baseline`) exist in code only.
- **3 prototypes**: one generic page shell (`main`) and two full templates (`product-listing`, `product-detail`), all React-in-browser, all explicitly unverified against Figma measurements.
- **0 screens, 0 flows, 0 requirements, 0 feedback entries** — none of those tracks have started.
- Neither the catalog nor the viewer is deployed to Vercel yet (`project.config.js` has empty `deployUrl` fields).
- Two open questions are sitting unresolved in `01-context/project-context.md` about whether the redesign keeps the current site's visual restraint or departs from it — that's a live ambiguity affecting every component built after this point.

## 7. How you'll actually use it as front-end lead

Right now (Design & Requirements Stage), your highest-value moves are: read specs + contract to understand the intended API before code exists elsewhere, sanity-check prototypes against the contract (run `validate.mjs`), and flag gaps like the `link` component early rather than at handover. Once `05-handover/index.md` flips to **"Ready for Build,"** your workflow becomes: start at that index, drill into the contract for exact attributes/slots/a11y per component, cross-reference the matching spec for design rationale and token usage, check the matching prototype for interaction behaviour, build the real component in your actual stack, and write your implementation notes into that spec's platform layer as you go.

## Level 2: the mechanics

**This is a template, not a bespoke build.** The repo you're in is one *instance* of a reusable system Accenture Song calls the "DDP Design OS." The same skeleton gets cloned for every client project. What makes it an "OS" rather than just a folder structure is three layers working together:

1. **Rules** — `CLAUDE.md` (what you already saw)
2. **Operations** — a set of slash-command "skills" that do the actual work
3. **State** — the numbered folders, which hold whatever the project has produced so far

### Two independent tracks

The workflow splits into two tracks that don't block each other:

- **Design track** (designer-triggered): raw input → tokens, component specs, screen specs, working prototypes
- **Requirements track** (BA/PM-triggered): scans whatever specs exist and generates epics/features/user stories

Zimmermann has only ever run the design track. There's no `03-requirements` or `04-feedback` folder in this repo yet, meaning no one has run `/requirements-scan` or `/capture-feedback`. That's not a gap, it's just a fact about how this project has been worked so far.

### What's actually in each folder here

| Folder | Purpose | State in this repo |
|---|---|---|
| `01-context` | Input side: raw client materials, workshop notes, a synthesized `project-context.md`, a running `decisions.md` | Populated, actively maintained |
| `02-design` | All design output. The biggest, most active folder | Mature: library, specs, prototypes, catalog, viewer all in use, plus an `ia/` (information architecture) and `shared/` folder specific to this project |
| `03-requirements` | BA/PM epics, features, stories | Doesn't exist. Requirements track never triggered |

| `05-handover` | The dev entry point, `index.md`, plus platform-specific guardrails | Populated, actively maintained (Build Status: **Design & Requirements Stage**, not yet frozen) |

### The engine: skills

Every action in this repo (pulling from Figma, writing a spec, building a prototype, assembling the handover) is done through a **skill**: a `.md` file under `.claude/skills/` that I read and follow like an operating procedure, invoked as a slash command (`/extract`, `/handover`, `/update-context`, etc.). Each skill has:

- One job

# Skill: /extract

Single entry point for all design extraction. Identifies what you have, explains what it will produce, and routes to the right process. Replaces `/extract-library`, `/extract-specs`, and `/extract-interaction`.

---

## Pre-flight: Check for incomplete sessions

Check memory for any incomplete `/extract` session. If found, surface it first:
> "[date]: An /extract session was not completed. Continue where you left off?"
Wait for response before proceeding.

---

## Pre-flight: Path resolution

Read `.claude/skills/_shared/portability.md` and resolve paths before scanning.

Required: `library`, `specs`
Optional: `contextProject`, `prototypes`

---

## Step 1: Get the source

Write a memory entry: "Skill /extract started [today's date], incomplete."

Ask: "Paste a Figma link, a URL (Storybook or live site), a local file path (JSON, CSS, SCSS, or Markdown), or type a prototype folder name. Say 'everything' to run a full extraction pass on all Figma sources."

---

## Step 2: Identify the source

Analyse what was pasted or typed. For Figma URLs, use the Figma MCP to read the frame structure before classifying.

**The distinction "library file vs design file" does not apply.** Any Figma file can be the source for tokens, components, or both. The frame's content determines the route, not the file it lives in.

| What was given | How to identify | Routes to |
|---|---|---|
| Figma tokens/styles frame | Frame contains colour swatches, typography scales, spacing values, or variable definitions. Primarily reference content with no interactive component set. | `library.md` (tokens mode) |
| Figma component frame | Named, bounded UI unit with variants, states, or a component set | Reusability assessment (see below) |
| Figma template or page frame | Full-screen layout with named structural regions (header, main, footer, or equivalent). Use Figma MCP to read the frame: placeholder content → Template; real content → Page. | `specs.md` (template) |
| Figma screen frame | Content-bearing UI screen or state, not a full page shell with structural regions. | `specs.md` (screen) |
| Figma flow frame | Flow or journey layout connecting multiple screens. | `specs.md` (flow) |
| Prototype folder name or path | Matches an existing folder under `/02-design/prototypes/`. Read its `intent.md` to check the `stage` field, then ask: "Interaction spec, template spec, or component/screen spec?" | `interaction.md` for interaction; `specs.md` (template) for `stage: template`; `specs.md` (Path B) for component or screen |
| Storybook URL | `https://` URL pointing to a hosted Storybook | `non-figma.md` (tokens) |
| Live website URL | `https://` URL pointing to a live site (not Figma, not Storybook). Ask: "Are you extracting tokens or documenting this as a spec?" | `non-figma.md` for tokens, `specs.md` (Path C) for spec |
| Image file (.png, .jpg) | Path to a local image file | `specs.md` (Path C), converted via MarkItDown (with OCR) if needed |
| PDF file | Path to a local PDF | `specs.md` (Path C), converted via MarkItDown |
| Word/Excel/PowerPoint (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) | Path to a document file | `specs.md` (Path C), converted via MarkItDown |
| JSON token file | Path to a `.json` file (Design Tokens, Style Dictionary, or custom format) | `non-figma.md` (tokens) |
| CSS or SCSS file | Path to a `.css` or `.scss` file | `non-figma.md` (tokens) |
| Markdown file | Path to a `.md` file containing token or component documentation | `non-figma.md` (tokens) |
| Written description or whiteboard photo | Plain text description or image of a sketch with no design tool source | `specs.md` (Path D) |
| "everything", "all", or no specific source | User wants a full extraction pass | Confirm, then run `library.md` (tokens) → `library.md` Mode C for each component frame → `interaction.md` (all prototypes) in sequence |

### Reusability assessment (component frames)

When a Figma frame is identified as a component frame, run this assessment before routing.

**Default assumption: it is reusable.** Any named, bounded UI component is a library candidate. The designer opts out rather than in.

**Determine the atomic tier** from the frame's layer structure and child components:

| Tier | Characteristics | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Atom | Single-purpose unit. No sub-components. Renders one thing. | Button, icon, input field, badge, tag, price label, avatar, checkbox, radio |
| Molecule | 2-5 atoms combined into one functional unit with a clear single job. | Search field, nav item, product card, form group, icon button, rating, wishlist toggle |
| Organism | Complex section with its own layout, composed of molecules and/or atoms. Occupies a full region of a page. | Navigation bar, site header, site footer, product grid, cart panel, mega menu, filter sidebar |

Read the frame structure: layer names, child component instances, and layout dimensions. Pick the lowest tier that fits. Don't over-promote.

**Surface the proposal:**

> "This looks like a [tier]: [one-line description of what it does and where it appears in a real build]. I'll extract it as a library element (Web Component + demo at `02-design/library/elements/[name]/`) and write a spec (`02-design/specs/components/[name].md`). That makes it usable in prototypes and ready for dev handover. Sound right, or should this be spec-only?"

Wait for the designer's response.

- **Confirmed (or any affirmative):** Route to `library.md` Mode C. One pass produces the library element and the spec.
- **Wrong tier:** Designer corrects the tier. Update and proceed.
- **Spec-only:** Route to `specs.md` Path A. No library element written.

---

## Step 3: Explain in plain English

Tell the user what you found and what you are about to produce. Keep it simple. Junior designers are the audience. Avoid jargon unless the user has clearly demonstrated familiarity.

**Figma component frame (reusable, library element + spec):**
> "That's a [tier]: [what it does]. I'll build it as a Web Component so it's usable in any prototype, and write a spec so developers can implement it. Files go into `02-design/library/elements/[name]/` and `02-design/specs/components/[name].md`."

**Figma component frame (spec-only):**
> "That's a component design. I'll document how it's built, what states and variants it has, and grab a screenshot. Output goes into `02-design/specs/components/`."

**Figma tokens/styles frame:**
> "That's your tokens/styles reference. I'll document all the colour, spacing, and typography values and write them as CSS custom properties. Output goes into `02-design/library/tokens.md` and `02-design/library/common.css`."

**Figma template or page frame:**
> "That's a [template / page]. I'll document the structural regions, component mapping per region, and responsive layout behaviour. Output goes into `02-design/specs/templates/`."

**Figma screen frame:**
> "That's a screen design. I'll document the layout, content, styles used, and interactive elements, and take a screenshot. Output goes into `02-design/specs/screens/`."

**Figma flow frame:**
> "That's a flow or navigation design. I'll document the screens, transitions, and connection logic, and take a screenshot. Output goes into `02-design/specs/flows/`."

**Prototype folder:**
> "That's the [folder name] prototype. I'll extract the interaction specs and update the linked spec file. I'll also check for any new styles that should be promoted to the shared library."

**Non-Figma source (Storybook URL, live site, JSON, CSS, SCSS, Markdown):**
> "That's a [source type]. I'll extract what I can: colours, typography, spacing, and any other named values. For URLs, expect some noise. I can only read what's publicly visible and can't always tell intentional tokens from utility styles or third-party injections. Everything starts as a candidate. You review, confirm, and I publish to `/02-design/library/`."

**Prototype (spec extraction):**
> "That's the [folder name] prototype. I'll check if a spec already exists for it. If it does, I'll point you there. If not, I'll read the code and produce a [component / screen / template] spec: token references, structure, behaviour intent, and any responsive layout notes from the prototype's intent file."

**Image, PDF, or live URL (spec extraction):**
> "That's a [image / PDF / URL]. I'll analyse what's visible and produce a spec with approximate layout, colours, and component structure. Values I can't measure precisely will be flagged as estimated. Same spec format, but treat flagged values as starting points to verify."

**Written description or whiteboard photo:**
> "Got it. No visual design values to extract here, so I'll produce a behaviour-focused spec: what the component or screen does, its states, variants, and any accessibility intent. Token values and layout will be left blank for a designer to fill in."

Then ask: "Is that what you're trying to do, or something different?"

---

## Step 4: Argue if intent doesn't match source

If the user confirms something that does not match what the source can produce, push back clearly. One push-back is enough. If the user insists after the explanation, proceed with their stated intent.

Examples:
- User pastes a component frame link but says they want tokens: "That link is a component, not a styles/variables frame. You won't get tokens from it. You'd get a library element and spec. Did you mean to paste your tokens frame link instead?"
- User names a prototype folder but says they want a component spec: "That's a local prototype folder, not a Figma frame. I can extract interaction specs from it, but not a component spec. For a component spec, paste a Figma link to the component frame instead."
- User pastes a screen frame but says they want a library element: "That link points to a screen, not a component. I can extract a screen spec from it, but not a library element. Paste a link to the specific component frame you want extracted."

---

## Step 5: Route

Once source and intent are confirmed, read and follow the instructions in the appropriate sub-file:

- **Reusable component (library element + spec):** read `.claude/skills/extract/library.md` and follow all steps (Mode C)
- **Tokens/styles extraction:** read `.claude/skills/extract/library.md` and follow all steps (Mode A or B)
- **Spec-only (screens, templates, flows, or spec-only components):** read `.claude/skills/extract/specs.md` and follow all steps
- **Interaction extraction:** read `.claude/skills/extract/interaction.md` and follow all steps
- **Non-Figma extraction:** read `.claude/skills/extract/non-figma.md` and follow all steps
- **Full pass:** run `library.md` (tokens, if a tokens frame exists or was identified) → `library.md` Mode C for each component frame found → `interaction.md` (all prototypes in `/02-design/prototypes/`) in sequence

---

## Step 6: Complete

**IA sync check:** If this run produced or modified any page-level, screen-level, or flow spec, and `02-design/ia/ia.md` exists, check whether the affected surfaces appear as nodes in `ia.md`. If any are missing or unlinked, note it at the end of your completion message:

> "New surfaces not yet in the IA: [list]. Run `/map-ia` to add them, or `/stitch-pages` to reconcile all at once."

If `ia.md` does not exist, skip this check silently.

Update the memory entry to: "Skill /extract completed [today's date]."

## Level 3: how `/extract` actually works, and the rule system underneath it

`/extract` is the single entry point for turning design work into library elements and specs. Two things make it more than "convert Figma to code":

### It identifies before it acts

Given a Figma link, URL, or file, it first classifies the source using a routing table, tokens frame vs. component frame vs. template/page frame vs. screen frame vs. flow frame vs. prototype folder vs. Storybook/live URL vs. document vs. plain description. Each type routes to a different sub-process. It never assumes; it reads the actual frame structure via the Figma MCP first.

### Everything defaults to reusable, and it explains before producing

If the source is a component, `/extract` runs a **reusability assessment**: the default assumption is "this is reusable," the designer opts out rather than in. It then classifies the component into a tier (below), states in plain English exactly what it's about to build and where the files will land, and waits for confirmation. If someone's stated intent doesn't match what the source can actually produce (e.g. pasting a screen link but asking for a reusable component), it pushes back once before proceeding.

Only after confirmation does it "route": read the relevant sub-file (`library.md`, `specs.md`, `interaction.md`, or `non-figma.md`) and execute those steps.

### The classification rule underneath it all: the atomic model

This is the part that matters most for you as the dev consuming the output. Every component gets sorted into one of five tiers, and the rule is mechanical, not a judgment call on visual complexity:

| Tier | Defined by |
|---|---|
| **Atom** | Renders no other component. Markup + CSS + tokens only. |
| **Molecule** | Renders only atoms. |
| **Organism** | Renders at least one molecule. |
| **Template** | Skeletal page frame, named regions, no real content. Renders at least one organism. |
| **Page** | A template instance with real content. |

The tier is decided by what a component's **own template renders**, recorded in the contract as `composes: [...]`. Some sharp edge rules worth knowing:

- **Icons are attributes, not components** (`icon="arrow-right"`), so a button with an icon is still an atom.
- **Slotted content doesn't change tier.** Only what a component renders itself counts, not what gets passed into it.
- **Template vs. Page is about real content vs. placeholder**, not complexity.
- **Only Atoms, Molecules, and Organisms become actual `zimm-*` Custom Elements with contract entries.** Templates and Pages are spec-only, they document layout intent (named regions, which components go where, responsive behavior), but you as the developer decide how to actually assemble them in React. They never generate a `.js` file.

This directly explains what you pulled in the last commit: the 6 new things (`zimm-page-toolbar`, `zimm-hero-blocks`, etc.) are real Custom Elements because they're atoms/molecules/organisms. The 2 new "product-listing" and "product-detail" **templates** are prototypes and specs only, there's no `zimm-product-listing-template.js` anywhere, because templates aren't delivered as components, by design.

This tier system is enforced mechanically by `02-design/library/contract/validate.mjs`, which checks the contract file for internal consistency against these exact rules.

Next up: the contract file itself (`zimm-contract.js`), which is the literal machine-readable source of truth you'd consume as the front-end lead. Say the word.

# Component contract

The contract is the single source of truth for the component API. Every component
that exists (its name, tier, attributes, slots, composition, and accessibility
requirements) is recorded here. If it is not in the contract, it does not exist.

---

## What is in this folder

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `[prefix]-contract.js` | The contract: an array of component definitions. Generated and maintained by `/extract`. |
| `validate.mjs` | Checks the atomic model rules against the contract. Run before any handover. |

---

## How to read a contract entry

```js
{
  name:      "Button",          // PascalCase component name
  prefix:    "ds",              // tag namespace (from project.config.js)
  element:   "ds-button",       // the custom element tag
  atomic:    "atom",            // atom | molecule | organism
  composes:  [],                // elements this component renders in its own template
  attributes: [
    { name: "variant", type: "enum",    values: ["primary","secondary","ghost"], default: "primary" },
    { name: "size",    type: "enum",    values: ["sm","md","lg"],                default: "md" },
    { name: "disabled",type: "boolean",                                          default: false },
  ],
  slots: [
    { name: "default", description: "Button label text" },
  ],
  a11y:      "role=button, aria-disabled when disabled, keyboard: Enter and Space activate",
  status:    "final",           // draft | in-review | final
  extracted: "2026-07-07",
}
```

**`atomic`**: the component's tier, determined by what it renders in its own template:
- `atom`: renders no other component. `composes: []`.
- `molecule`: renders only atoms.
- `organism`: renders at least one molecule.

`template` and `page` are not valid contract tiers. They are layout-layer deliverables, not Custom Elements. See atomic model Rule F in `.claude/skills/_shared/atomic-model.md`.

**`composes`**: what the component's own template renders. Slotted children are not listed here (see atomic model Rule B). This determines the tier and build order: build atoms first, then molecules, then organisms.

**`attributes`**: the component's public API. These map directly to `observedAttributes` in the Custom Element. Types:
- `enum`: a fixed set of values. Use the `default` if none is passed or the value is unrecognised.
- `boolean`: present = true, absent = false.
- `string`: freeform content.

**`slots`**: named `"default"` is the element's child content. Named slots use `slot="[name]"` on a child element.

---

## How to implement a component

1. Read the contract entry for your component.
2. Build one Custom Element per entry. The `element` value is the tag to register.
3. `composes` → your imports. Build those components first.
4. `attributes` → your `observedAttributes` array and prop defaults.
5. `slots` → your shadow DOM slot elements.
6. `a11y` → bake in. Assert in tests.
7. All styles reference CSS custom properties from `02-design/library/common.css`.
   No hardcoded values.

## Definition of done (per component)

- One Custom Element matching the contract API
- All `observedAttributes` match the contract `attributes` list
- All slots match the contract `slots` list
- `composes` matches what the template actually renders
- No props or imports beyond the contract entry
- Light and dark themes verified
- `node 02-design/library/contract/validate.mjs` passes with no violations

---

## Adding a new component

If a design needs a component not in the contract, **stop and flag it** as a proposed
addition. Do not invent a component, attribute, or token outside the contract. Raising
it means agreeing on the API, classifying the tier, extracting it via `/extract`, and
adding the entry here.

---

## Running the validator

```sh
node 02-design/library/contract/validate.mjs
```

Checks contract integrity and scans all `demo.html` files for unknown element tags.
Exit 0 = clean. Exit 1 = violations listed.

## Level 4: the contract, the actual thing you'll build against

The philosophy here is blunt: **"If it is not in the contract, it does not exist."** `zimm-contract.js` is one exported array, one object per component, and it is the literal API surface you implement to. It's generated and maintained only by `/extract`, not hand-edited.

### A real entry, from this repo

```js
{
  name: "Icon",
  prefix: "zimm",
  element: "zimm-icon",
  atomic: "atom",
  composes: [],
  attributes: [
    { name: "type", type: "enum", values: ["arrow-down", ... 33 more], default: "menu" },
    { name: "size", type: "enum", values: ["20","16","12"], default: "20" },
  ],
  slots: [],
  a11y: "Inner img has role=img and aria-label from type name. Set aria-hidden=true on the host when decorative.",
  status: "draft",
  extracted: "2026-07-08",
}
```

Each field has one job:
- **`element`**: the actual custom element tag you register (`<zimm-icon>`)
- **`composes`**: what this component's own template renders. This is both the tier proof (empty = atom) and your build order: build everything in `composes` before you build this one.
- **`attributes`**: maps directly to `observedAttributes` on your Custom Element. This *is* the public API, nothing more, nothing less.
- **`a11y`**: not a suggestion, a requirement to bake in and test against.
- **`status`**: draft → in-review → final. Right now, Zimmermann's whole contract is still `draft` (one `placeholder`), nothing has been marked final yet, consistent with the project still sitting in Design & Requirements Stage.

### Where Zimmermann's contract stands today

27 components total: **14 atoms, 10 molecules, 3 organisms**. No templates or pages in here, by design, they're spec-only (Level 3).

### It's mechanically enforced, not just documented

`validate.mjs` is a real Node script (140 lines), not a checklist. Run it as:

```sh
node 02-design/library/contract/validate.mjs
```

It does two checks:
1. **Contract integrity**: rejects any entry tiered as `template` or `page` outright (hard-coded rule), checks every tier is valid, and checks every `composes` reference actually resolves to a real entry in the contract, not a typo or a deleted component.
2. **Conformance**: scans every `demo.html` under `02-design/library/elements/` for custom element tags in use, and flags any tag that doesn't resolve back to a contract entry. So an undocumented element quietly used in a demo gets caught.

Exit 0 = clean, exit 1 = violations printed.

### Why this matters to you specifically

The contract's README defines "definition of done" per component, and it's exactly what you'll be graded against at build time: your Custom Element's `observedAttributes` must match the contract's `attributes` 1:1, your slots must match 1:1, `composes` must match what your template *actually* renders, no extra props or imports beyond the entry, and `validate.mjs` passes clean. If you need a component during build that isn't in the contract, the protocol isn't to just build it, it's to stop and flag it as a proposed addition, since inventing one outside this file breaks the "single source of truth" guarantee the whole handover depends on.

Next up: the prototypes/viewer system (how designers demonstrate interaction and how it gets deployed), or the versioning/changelog convention used across every file. Say the word.

## Level 5: prototypes and the viewer

### Prototypes are real running code, not mockups

Checked the actual `product-detail` template prototype we pulled last commit: it loads the real `zimm-*` Custom Elements directly as ES modules straight from the shared library:

```html
<script type="module" src="../../../library/elements/product-detail/zimm-product-detail.js">
<script type="module" src="../../../library/elements/navigation/zimm-navigation.js">
```

So when a stakeholder clicks through a prototype in a browser, they're running the literal same component code that lives in the contract, not a separate design-only recreation. One non-obvious thing worth knowing: `project.config.js` declares `prototypeStack: "react-cdn"` as the default build approach for scaffolding *new* prototypes, but the library elements themselves are plain vanilla Custom Elements, framework-agnostic by construction. That's exactly why they drop into a React-CDN prototype, a vanilla one, or eventually your real React build equally well, and why the target stacks list both `web` and `react` against the same components.

### The intent.md contract for a prototype

Every prototype folder carries an `intent.md` with frontmatter (`spec`, `stack`, `stage`, viewer metadata) and four body sections: **Why**, **What**, **Fidelity**, **Components referenced**. The Fidelity field is an honesty check worth trusting: the product-detail prototype is flagged `hi-fi, ... Wired in Claude, measurements not confirmed from Figma`. That's the repo telling you, explicitly, this is a strong approximation, not something pixel-verified against source Figma. Good to remember before treating any prototype's spacing as gospel.

### The viewer: one shell, all content-driven

Two files move together every time a prototype gets registered:
- `02-design/prototypes/INDEX.md`, a human-readable log
- `02-design/viewer/viewer.config.js`, the actual runtime config the viewer app reads

Both are written in the same pass by `/add-to-viewer`, never by hand (confirmed: both list `templates/product-detail`, registered `2026-07-17`, label "Product Detail", identically). The viewer shell itself (`02-design/viewer/index.html`) is never touched per-project, it's deliberately generic and reused across every Design OS project; all customization is just data in `viewer.config.js`. Same code/content split you saw with the contract. There's also a `setup.html` in that folder, a visual tool you open directly in Chrome to reorder, relabel, or regroup prototypes without hand-editing JS.

### Where this actually lives right now

`/deploy-viewer` is the skill that connects this to Vercel so every `git push` auto-deploys one shareable client-facing URL. For Zimmermann specifically: `vercel.json` already exists and is more built out than the skill's own minimal starter template, it also routes `/catalog`, `/ia`, `/library`, `/shared`, and `/prototypes` directly. But `project.config.js` still has `deployUrl` commented out. **That means `/deploy-viewer` has never actually been completed here, there's no live public URL for this viewer yet.** Someone set up the routing groundwork but never finished connecting an actual Vercel project. Worth knowing if a client asks for a link.

Remaining threads I haven't covered: the `/handover` skill itself (how `05-handover/index.md` and the per-platform guardrail docs get assembled, the actual thing you'll open as a developer), the versioning/changelog convention used across every file, or the other skills (`/workshop`, `/update-context`, `/map-ia`, `/requirements-scan`). Given your role, handover is probably the natural next stop, but say which one.

10	## Key platform constraints for designers
11

## Level 6: `/handover`, and a real gap I found by cross-checking it

### What `/handover` actually does

It's not a separate mechanism, it's an **orchestrator**. It runs the exact same `/extract` sub-processes you already know (library, specs, interactions) across the *entire* repo in one pass, then generates `05-handover/index.md`, optionally exports a BMAD-compatible format, then makes one summary commit. It's explicitly framed as "a milestone snapshot, not a lock", rerunnable at any sprint end without fear of breaking something.

### The index, by the numbers

`05-handover/index.md` is one table-of-contents file, changelog at the top (last 5 entries, full history in GitHub), cross-linking tokens → components → contract → screens/flows/templates → prototypes → requirements → platform. Reading the actual current state:

- **27 components**, all still `draft` or `placeholder` status, none `final`
- **0 screens, 0 flows**, one template with a real prototype
- **0 requirements** (epics/features/stories all zero, confirms the requirements track has genuinely never run)
- **Platform guardrails: only `web` exists**, no `react/` folder yet, despite `react` being a listed target stack

### A real gap, not a hypothetical one

I cross-referenced the new `product-detail` prototype against the index rather than taking either at face value, and found a genuine inconsistency worth knowing before you trust this repo's "spec coverage":

The `product-detail` prototype's own `intent.md` declares `spec: screens/product-detail.md`, that's the spec file it's supposed to feed into. But `02-design/specs/screens/` is empty (only a `.gitkeep`). The handover index says so itself: **"Screens: No screen specs yet."** The prototype and its components got built and registered, but the written screen spec they're supposed to document into never got created.

Same pattern in the Components tables: **12 of the 27 components have a blank Spec column** (`zimm-select`, `zimm-search`, `zimm-card-baseline`, `zimm-cat-links-aside`, `zimm-page-toolbar`, `zimm-input-action`, `zimm-search-overlay`, `zimm-toolbar-category`, `zimm-hero-blocks`, `zimm-product-detail-gallery`, `zimm-product-detail-options`, `zimm-product-detail`).

**Practical takeaway for you:** "it's in the handover index" does not mean "it's fully spec'd." The contract (`zimm-contract.js`) is mechanically enforced by `validate.mjs`, so it's reliable as an API source of truth. The prose specs are patchier right now, always check whether a component's Spec column actually links somewhere before treating it as build-ready documentation, rather than assuming index presence equals completeness.

### The platform layer: your actual folder

`05-handover/platform/web/README.md` is the concrete "platform layer" from the two-layer spec model (design layer = never touch, platform layer = dev-owned, added after handover). It currently defines: breakpoints (360 / 768 / 1280 / 1440px), a browser degradation matrix (e.g. `:has()` → JS class toggle fallback, container queries → media query fallback), an accessibility checklist, and confirmation that web specs reference CSS custom properties from `common.css` directly, no separate token-mapping layer needed. There's a sibling `annotation-template.md` for logging spec deviations once you start building. Only `web/` exists so far; if this project ever needs React-specific guardrails beyond the shared web ones, that folder doesn't exist yet and would need to be created.

That closes the main spine: context → design → extract → contract → prototypes → viewer → handover → platform. Remaining loose threads, if you want full coverage: the versioning/changelog convention (small), the still-unused skills (`/workshop`, `/update-context`, `/map-ia`, `/requirements-scan`, `/stitch-pages`, `/capture-feedback`), or the governance rules in `CLAUDE.md` itself (missing-path protocol, prompt-injection guard, conversational intake table). Say which, or say "wrap it up" for a one-pass summary of everything.

## ELI5: how you, specifically, use this

You have two modes, and which one you're in depends entirely on that `Build Status` field.

**Mode 1, right now (Design & Requirements Stage): you're a reader, not a builder.**

Your front door is `05-handover/index.md`. Open it, it links to everything: components, specs, contract, prototypes. Right now your job is just to stay oriented and sanity-check, not to build production code against any of it, because it can still change under you. Concretely:

**Mode 2, later (Build Status flips to "Ready for Build"): that's your green light.**

From that point on, your entire build loop is mechanical, one component at a time:
1. Open its entry in `zimm-contract.js`, that's your exact spec: attributes, slots, composition, accessibility requirements.

Good ticket to use, because the repo doesn't fully cover it yet, which is exactly where you'd actually have to *do* something rather than just read. Here's what actually exists versus what this ticket needs.

## What's already in the repo for this surface

`zimm-product-detail-options` (a molecule, composing `zimm-button` + `zimm-select` + `zimm-add-to-wishlist`) already renders the size row and the Add to Bag button:

```js
<zimm-select placeholder="Size" options='${sizeOptions}'></zimm-select>
...
<zimm-button variant="primary" size="large" label="${ctaLabel}" full-width></zimm-button>
```

That's it. It's a plain dropdown of sizes and an always-enabled button. I checked, and none of this ticket's actual behavior exists anywhere in the repo yet: zero hits anywhere in `02-design/` or `01-context/` for "notify," "low stock," "limited availability," "coming soon," or "one size." The one thing that *is* already there and reusable: `zimm-button`'s contract already has a `disabled: boolean` attribute, so the CTA atom has the plumbing, it's just not wired to anything yet.

This lines up exactly with the Jira comments on the ticket: Jasmijn split "Coming Soon / Unavailable" into its own story, and design for the one-size layout, the low-stock indicator, and add-to-bag state management were only signed off today. Nothing here is a gap you missed, it genuinely hasn't been extracted into this repo yet.

## How you'd actually work this, step by step

**1. Don't start coding SFCC/React yet. This is an `/extract` job first.**
This repo's rule is "if it's not in the contract, it does not exist", so before you touch a real template, the new size-selector states need to become a real library element with a contract entry. Since the ticket's attachment is a flattened PNG (`image-20260701-120944.png`), not a live Figma link, I'd flag that back: a flat image gets you lower-fidelity output ("estimated" values you'd have to verify), a live Figma frame gets you the real thing. Worth asking Jasmijn/Charmaine for the actual frame link before running `/extract`.

**2. Expect `/extract` to propose splitting this into a new atom, and reclassifying the parent.**
Per the atomic model (Level 3), a single size option with three states (available, unavailable-with-notify-me, low-stock) is a new **atom**. Once `ProductDetailOptions` composes that atom via a new **SizeSelector molecule** instead of a plain `zimm-select`, `ProductDetailOptions` stops being a molecule itself, an organism composing a molecule is the definition of an organism. That's not a hypothetical, it's the mechanical rule from `atomic-model.md` actually applying to a real ticket. Expect `/extract` to surface that reclassification and ask you to confirm it.

**3. Map each AC to where it actually lives, because not all of it belongs in this repo.**

| AC | Where it's handled |
|---|---|
| Sizes render, in-stock sizes selectable | New size-option states in the library element |
| Single size ⇒ no selector, just shows the one size | New variant/mode on that same component |
| Unavailable size ⇒ not selectable + inline Notify Me | New state, this repo (Notify Me *slide-out* itself is explicitly a separate story) |
| Low/Limited Availability indicator | New state. Note: the ticket text says "Low Availability" but Jasmijn's later comment says it "should be Limited Availability", flag that naming conflict now so the contract doesn't get built with the wrong enum value |
| CTA disabled until size selected | Wiring `zimm-button`'s existing `disabled` attribute to selection state, component logic, not a new atom |
| "Please select a size" message on click | Likely a new inline validation state, worth checking during extraction whether `zimm-select` or `zimm-text-input` already has an error-message pattern to reuse instead of inventing a new one |
| Inventory-driven availability, cart integration | **Out of scope for this repo entirely.** That's real data/API wiring in your actual SFCC app, sitting outside the contract and spec altogether |

**4. Once the contract entry and spec exist, that's when your normal build loop kicks in**: read the contract entry, build the SFCC/React component matching it exactly, wire your own inventory logic around the states the design system now exposes, run `validate.mjs`, done.

**One thing worth naming plainly:** this project's `Build Status` still says "Design & Requirements Stage," but you've clearly got a real sprint ticket with a linked SFCC story ready to be picked up. In practice, delivery is running ahead of that status flag. That's fine, it just means for tickets like this, you can't lean on "wait for Ready for Build," you have to do exactly what we just did: check the actual repo contents against the ticket by hand before you build anything.

Direct answer: **there's no pipeline.** No code, build step, or CI/CD connects this repo to your actual SFCC/React storefront repo. The bridge is entirely the contract + spec + prototype, read by a human, then re-implemented in the real codebase. Nothing here gets literally shipped by default.

## What actually crosses over, and what gets rebuilt

| Artifact here | What happens in the real repo |
|---|---|
| **Tokens** (`common.css` custom properties) | Most directly portable. These are literally the CSS values, they typically get copied or regenerated into the app's own token/stylesheet system so colours/spacing match exactly. |
| **Contract entry** (attributes, slots, `composes`, a11y) | Becomes the required API your real component must expose, in whatever form your actual stack uses (React props, SFRA/ISML template params, etc.). Not copied, translated. |
| **Written spec** (markdown) | Becomes your behavior/acceptance reference, states, variants, rationale. |
| **Prototype** (working demo) | Becomes the literal visual and interaction reference to match against, and it's useful for QA/visual comparison since it's real running behavior, not a static mock. |
| **The `.js` Custom Element file itself** | *Maybe* reusable as-is, *maybe* not. Depends entirely on what your production storefront actually is. |

That last row is the one worth sitting with, because it's the real open question for your team.

## Why the last row is ambiguous

`project.config.js` lists **both** `web` and `react` as target stacks. Those imply two different answers:

- If your Zimmermann storefront is a server-rendered SFRA/ISML setup (or any plain-DOM frontend), Custom Elements are a browser standard, no framework required, so the exact `.js` files in `02-design/library/elements/` could genuinely be vendored in and used as-is.
- If it's a React-based composable storefront (e.g. PWA Kit), teams usually don't want raw Custom Elements sitting inside a React tree, they rebuild an idiomatic React component with matching props, using the contract as the spec, not the file as the source.

The contract's own instructions back this up, they say "build one Custom Element per entry" as a generic instruction, not "copy this file", because the target stack was never assumed to be fixed. Nothing I've seen in this repo settles which path your actual SFCC setup takes, that's a real decision for you and whoever owns the storefront architecture, not something the Design OS dictates.

## Where the mapping decision actually gets written down

This isn't left implicit. Recall the two-layer spec model: every spec has a **platform layer**, dev-owned, added after handover, and its explicit job is "component mapping to target stack, deviations from spec with reasons." That's the literal place you'd record, per component, "here's our SFCC/React equivalent, here's where it deviates from the contract and why." It lives in the same spec file, just a section you own instead of design.

## Two entirely separate deployments, too

Worth being explicit: this repo's viewer and catalog deploy to Vercel (or would, once `/deploy-viewer` actually finishes, still not done here). That's a reference site for stakeholders. Your production storefront deploys to SFCC's own infrastructure. Completely separate hosting, separate pipelines, separate everything. A push to this repo never touches production.

## And nothing checks the two stay in sync

`validate.mjs` only validates this repo against itself, contract entries against `demo.html` files that live here. It never runs against your app repo. Once you've built the real component, keeping it matched to the contract is manual developer discipline, there's no automated gate enforcing it across the boundary. If the contract changes after you've built against it, you find out by someone telling you, not by a CI failure in your app repo.
